1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5.name: Petrov's Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5.background: Of White's two main third moves it is the more popular, ahead of 3.d4.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6.name: Petrov's Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6.background: Carl Jaenisch highlighted Alexander Petrov's independent rediscovery of Cozio's 3.Nxe5 d6, played in preference to 3...Qd7.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6.strategy: Attacks the knight on e5 and so drives it away before Black retakes the pawn. This is the sound way to equalise: once the knight has left the e-file, Black can take on e4 without running into tactics. The game is close to level, with White holding a small initiative.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 Nxe4.name: Petrov's Defence: Damiano Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 Nxe4.background: Introduced by Pedro Damiano in his Libro da Imparare a Giocare a Scacchi, one of the oldest books on "modern rules" chess. It is usually regarded as an error, though it has occasionally been seen in recent grandmaster play.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 Nxe4.strategy: Retakes at once, but the open e-file bites: the queen attacks e4 from e2, and a knight move uncovers a discovered check, so the natural-looking ...Nf6 loses the queen to Nc6+. Black has to find the exact defence, after which the game is about level; a slip loses at once.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 Nc6.name: Petrov's Defence: Stafford Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 Nc6.background: Named after Joseph Stafford, a correspondence player who won a notable six-move game with it in 1950. The earliest recorded game is from an 1857 simultaneous exhibition by Howard Staunton, who lost it as Black. It remained obscure until the early 2020s, when Eric Rosen's games made it popular in online blitz.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 Nc6.strategy: Offers the e-pawn for an open d-file, an active c8 bishop and an immediate attack on e4, aimed at White's kingside. If White replies calmly, Black has no real compensation for the pawn, but many natural-looking moves for White run into tactics.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3.name: Petrov's Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3.strategy: Brings the knight back to its best square, where it covers the centre and the kingside. Black takes the e4 pawn, material is level, and the question becomes whether White can drive the advanced Black knight away at an acceptable price.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nd3.name: Petrov's Defence: Karklins-Martinovsky Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nd3.background: Called the Karklins-Martinovsky Variation; the US master Andrew Karklins experimented with it. Magnus Carlsen played it against Fabiano Caruana in the 2018 World Chess Championship match.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nd3.strategy: Withdraws the knight to d3, where it blocks the d-pawn for now but heads for f4, and avoids the heavily analysed main line. Black simply takes the e4 pawn with equality: the move is sound, but it spends time and gives White no real edge.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nc4.name: Petrov's Defence: Paulsen Attack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nc4.background: De Firmian called it "ineffective", though it is occasionally seen at grandmaster level.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nc4.strategy: Retreats to c4, which keeps the d-pawn free to advance, but the knight is awkwardly placed there: once Black has taken on e4, ...d5 drives it away again and White loses time. Sound but ineffective, the knight usually ends up on e3.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nxf7.name: Petrov's Defence: Cochrane Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nxf7.background: Nick de Firmian called it “speculative but entertaining” in Modern Chess Openings, and judged the position of Topalov–Kramnik, Linares 1999, to offer chances for both sides.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nxf7.strategy: Gives a knight for a pawn to drag the king out: it can no longer castle, and White hopes to use the initiative and quick development against it. The compensation is speculative, because a piece is a lot to give and Black is clearly ahead if the attack runs out.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4.name: Petrov's Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4.strategy: Retakes the pawn now that the e-file is clear, restoring material equality and putting the knight on an active central square. White will try to chase it away or undermine it, and Black's task is to support the knight and keep a solid centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece but ignores the e4 pawn, which White simply defends, for example with the other knight. White has then won a clean pawn, and taking on e4 now loses a piece, since White recaptures and Black cannot retake.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Bg4.strategy: Pins the f3 knight against the queen, but White defends e4 and the pin changes nothing: if Black trades on f3, the queen recaptures and guards e4 itself. Black has lost the chance to regain the pawn and stays a pawn down.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.name: Petrov's Defence: Classical Attack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.background: The most popular fifth move for White, and the main line of the Classical Variation.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.strategy: Takes the centre and prepares to challenge the advanced knight with the bishop. Black supports it with a pawn, and the symmetrical structures that follow give White a small initiative but little more. The principal choice, because it fights for space instead of hurrying to trade.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.name: Petrov's Defence: Nimzowitsch Attack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.background: The chief sideline to 5.d4. Viswanathan Anand resigned after only six moves against Alonso Zapata at Biel 1988, having fallen for a trap in this line.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.strategy: Offers to trade the e4 knight and goes for rapid development: after the trade White recaptures with the d-pawn, which opens the queen and the c1 bishop and allows castling queenside for an attack on the kingside. White accepts doubled c-pawns for the initiative. Black must avoid ...Bf5??, which loses a piece to Qe2.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.name: Petrov's Defence: Cozio Attack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.background: The most common continuation at the amateur level.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.strategy: Pins the knight to the king along the open e-file, so Black has to unpin and defend with the queen; defending with a pawn instead loses the knight to d3. The game then heads for an early queen trade and a drawish endgame in which neither side has much to play for.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.name: Petrov's Defence: French Attack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.strategy: Kicks the knight away with a pawn at once. Black retreats it without loss, and White usually follows with d4 to build a symmetrical centre; the d-pawn has moved twice for the knight's two moves, so the tempi cancel out and the game is level and quiet.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.name: Petrov's Defence: Kaufmann Attack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.strategy: Takes the d5 square away from Black's pawn, so the knight cannot be supported there once d4 and the bishop arrive. The plan is slow, and Black simply withdraws the knight to a safe square or develops and challenges the centre, reaching equality.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.name: Petrov's Defence: Millennium Attack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.strategy: Attacks the knight directly with a developing move, but the bishop blocks White's own d-pawn and has to move again before the centre can be built. Black retreats the knight and White's structure is awkward, so the move is rarely played.

Supports the knight with a pawn, grabs the centre and opens the c8 bishop. It is the standard reply, giving Black a solid, symmetrical structure; White's task is to dislodge the advanced knight, Black's to keep it safe.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.name: Petrov's Defence: Classical Attack, Closed Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.strategy: A quiet retreat: the knight goes home and White keeps the more advanced d-pawn, so Black has given up active play and White keeps the first-move initiative. Sound but passive.

Develops the king's bishop and prepares to castle, leaving the knight on e4 for the moment. It reaches the same kind of symmetrical position as the main line and is the sound second choice; Black can still support the knight with the d-pawn when it is attacked.

Attacks the knight and prepares to castle. White will now try to drive the advanced knight away by adding pressure on it, which usually costs a structural concession that balances out the gain. The position is symmetrical, but Black has made one extra knight move.

Develops with an attack on the e4 knight. If Black trades, the bishop recaptures and White has a free development in a level, symmetrical position; but the knight on d2 blocks the c1 bishop until then, and the pawn on d5 keeps the black knight safe.
Prepares to castle without committing the bishop to d3, but it does not challenge the knight on e4, so Black gets time to complete development with the knight in place. Sound but unambitious.

Develops the bishop to its safest square and prepares to castle, giving the king shelter before White starts to undermine the advanced knight. It is the most solid set-up, though the bishop is passive on e7.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.name: Petrov's Defence: Classical Attack, Mason-Showalter Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.strategy: Develops the knight with pressure on d4 and prepares to castle. The game normally reaches the same positions as the quieter bishop move, since Black wants both, but Black keeps the choice of where the bishop goes.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.name: Petrov's Defence: Classical Attack, Marshall Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.background: Named after Frank Marshall, who played 8...Bg4 in it.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.strategy: Puts the bishop on the diagonal towards White's king, where it eyes h2, and keeps the position fully symmetrical. More active than the quiet bishop move, and the game stays balanced.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nxf7 Kxf7.strategy: Takes the knight: Black accepts the sacrifice and stands a piece up for two pawns. The cost is the king, dragged out of its corner and unable to castle, so Black's task is to bring it to safety and, if need be, give material back, while White plays for the initiative.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nxf7 Qd7.strategy: Attacks the knight with the queen, but the knight takes the rook on h8 first. Black is left chasing a knight in the corner at the cost of a rook.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nxf7 Nxe4.strategy: Grabs a pawn and ignores the knight on f7, which takes the queen on d8. Black recaptures with the king, but queen for knight is a lopsided trade and the extra pawn is no consolation.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nxf7 Kxf7.name: Petrov's Defence: Cochrane Gambit, Bishop Check Line
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nxf7 Kxf7.strategy: Checks to keep the king in the open, but the check is easily met: ...d5 blocks it and hits the bishop with a pawn, after which Black untangles the king and White has lost the pace the attack needs.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nxf7 Kxf7.name: Petrov's Defence: Cochrane Gambit, Centre Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nxf7 Kxf7.strategy: Takes the centre and opens the c1-bishop while the king is stranded. It leaves e4 undefended, but grabbing it is risky: ...Nxe4 allows Qh5+, and after ...g6 Qd5+ attacks king and knight together. Playable, but it hurries and gives Black time to organise the defence.

The best way to play the gambit: it develops a piece, defends e4 and keeps the bishop check and the central advance in hand rather than spending them early. White is still a piece down for two pawns, so it must make the stranded king count.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 Nc6 4.Nxc6.strategy: Takes the offered knight and keeps the extra pawn. Trading pieces brings the side that is ahead closer to consolidating its lead. The recapture opens lines for Black, so White must now look after e4 and the king's side.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 Nc6 4.d4.strategy: Declines the trade and takes the centre, with a pawn behind the knight on e5. Black can win the pawn back, so White hands back most of the advantage the pawn gave and keeps only a small edge.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 Nc6 4.Nf3.strategy: Retreats the knight and returns the pawn at once, since ...Nxe4 restores material. It is safe and avoids the gambit's tricks, but the game is level and White has thrown away the whole advantage.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 Nc6 4.Nxc6 dxc6.name: Petrov's Defence: Stafford Gambit Accepted
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 Nc6 4.Nxc6 dxc6.strategy: The point of the gambit: Black gives up a pawn and accepts doubled c-pawns to open the d-file for the queen and the diagonal for the c8-bishop. The pawn on e4 is already attacked and undefended, so White has to react at once.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 Nc6 4.Nxc6 bxc6.strategy: Recaptures with the b-pawn, which is playable but leaves the d-pawn at home, so neither the queen nor the c8-bishop gets any room. Black stays a pawn down without the lead in development that is the point of the gambit.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 Nc6 4.Nxc6 Nxe4.strategy: Takes a pawn and ignores the knight on c6, which takes the queen on d8. Black recaptures with the king, but has lost the queen for a pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 Nc6 4.Nxc6 dxc6.strategy: The solid answer: a pawn guards e4, the c1-bishop is freed, and White gives back nothing. The set-up looks passive, but it keeps the extra pawn and leaves Black to prove the compensation, while White has to avoid the tactics that centre on f2.

Defends e4 with a developing piece and leaves the d-pawn free. It is less solid than the pawn defence: a bishop on c5 and a knight on g4 can aim at f2 together, so White has to watch the kingside while the extra pawn is consolidated.

Drives the knight from f6 and takes space, but the knight lands on e4 and still presses on f2. White must then be exact: after 6.d3? Bc5 Black threatens ...Bxf2+ and ...Bg4 mate. It gives up much of White's advantage for a risky try.

Guards e4 and takes g4 away from the black knight in one move, so the usual pressure on f2 never starts. The cost is a loosened king's side, and Black, with a free bishop and the lead in development, still has play for the pawn.
Defends e4 with the queen, though on an awkward square in front of the f1-bishop. It works only if White avoids hasty pawn moves: a push to e5 runs into ...Ng4 and a crushing attack on f2.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 Nc6 4.Nxc6 dxc6.name: Petrov's Defence: Stafford Gambit Accepted
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 Nc6 4.Nxc6 dxc6.strategy: Aims the bishop at f2, which only the king guards, and turns natural developing moves into traps: after 6.Bg5? Nxe4! the queen is attacked and 7.Bxd8 Bxf2+ 8.Ke2 Bg4 is mate. Black's compensation rests on such quick tactics, not on structure.
Develops with tempo: the bishop attacks the queen, and taking it loses the queen to the knight. But White can simply trade the bishop off, and without it Black's compensation for the pawn thins out.
A calm developing move: the bishop is safe and covers c4 and a2, but it does nothing about f2. Black gives up the quick attack the gambit is built on and must hope to regain the pawn in a slow game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 Nc6 4.Nxc6 dxc6.name: Petrov's Defence: Stafford Gambit Accepted
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 Nc6 4.Nxc6 dxc6.strategy: The same idea against a different set-up: the bishop pressures f2, where only the king stands guard, and ...Ng4 can add a second attacker. With the knight on c3 the d-pawn is still free, but White must find a way to consolidate.

A quiet developing move: the bishop covers c4 and d5, but leaves f2 alone, so the gambit's pressure on the king's side is put aside. Black is then simply a pawn down in a slow game, which is not what the gambit is for.

Attacks the queen, and taking the bishop loses the queen to the knight, so White must spend a move on it. White can trade the bishop or kick it away, and either takes the force out of the attack on f2.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 Nxe4 4.Qe2.strategy: Attacks the knight and lines the queen up on the open e-file behind it. If the knight runs, White's knight can move with a discovered check, which is why ...Nf6?? loses at once to Nc6+, winning the queen. Black has to find the best defence.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 Nxe4 4.d4.strategy: Plants a pawn in the centre and supports the knight on e5, so ...d6 is met by a retreat that reaches a standard, level position. White gives up the chance to punish the early knight capture.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 Nxe4 4.Qf3.strategy: More of a trap than a plan: queen and knight both aim at f7, so the careless ...d5 loses to Qxf7 mate. Black just retreats the knight, material is level, and White has gained nothing for the early queen move, though it risks little.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 Nxe4 4.Qe2 Qe7.name: Petrov's Defence: Damiano Variation, Kholmov Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 Nxe4 4.Qe2 Qe7.background: Pedro Damiano gave 4.Qe2 Qe7 in his Libro da Imparare a Giocare a Scacchi, one of the oldest books on chess under the modern rules; the line now bears the name of the Kholmov Gambit.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 Nxe4 4.Qe2 Qe7.strategy: Black's best reply: the queen steps onto the e-file, so that after White takes the knight on e4 the white knight on e5 is pinned to its queen and can be hit with ...d6. Black ends a pawn down for open lines and quick development; White keeps a modest edge.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 Nxe4 4.Qe2 Nf6.strategy: The classic beginner's blunder: the knight retreats, and White's knight moves with a discovered check from the queen while also attacking the black queen. Black loses the queen for a knight.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 Nxe4 4.Qe2 d6.strategy: Counter-attacks the knight on e5, but White takes on e4 first: after 5.Qxe4 dxe5 6.Qxe5+ Black is a pawn down and has a check to answer.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 Nxe4 4.Qe2 d5.strategy: Defends the knight with a pawn, but the pin on the e-file remains. White attacks the knight again, the queens come off and Black is left a clean pawn down in an endgame.
